gaps.sentence: That's the boy ___ dog won first prize at the show.
gaps.hint: the dog belongs to the boy
gaps.explanation: 'Whose dog' means 'his dog'; 'who's' would mean 'who is', which makes no sense here.

gaps.sentence: It is one of the most impressive buildings ___ I have ever seen.
gaps.explanation: After superlative expressions, 'that' is the standard relative pronoun in defining clauses.

gaps.sentence: There are times ___ I really miss my home town.
gaps.explanation: 'There are times when ...' is a standard pattern; 'when' stands for 'at which'.

gaps.sentence: Is there a reason ___ you're behaving so strangely?
gaps.explanation: 'A reason why ...' asks about the cause; the other relative words cannot express reason.

gaps.sentence: She told me ___ had happened, but I didn't believe her.
gaps.explanation: 'What had happened' means 'the things that had happened'; 'that' cannot stand alone as the subject here.

gaps.sentence: The exam, the results of ___ will be published on Friday, was very difficult.
gaps.hint: quantity noun + of + thing in a non-defining clause
gaps.explanation: 'The results of which' joins the clauses formally; 'of whom' is for people and 'of them' cannot link clauses after a comma.
'What caused the fire' means 'the thing that caused it'; 'that' cannot act as the subject of this nominal clause.

gaps.sentence: This clock, ___ belonged to my grandmother, is still working perfectly.
gaps.hint: thing as subject; clause between commas
gaps.explanation: The clock is a thing, so 'which' is correct; 'that' cannot be used in a non-defining clause.
